# Before the First Lab {.unnumbered}

This chapter is for the reader who has never played Factorio — or never
run FISL. It contains everything the course assumes about your hands and
your machine, and nothing else. If you already play Factorio and have
run `fisl run` once, skip straight to Lab 0.

## What you need

- **Factorio**, the game (factorio.com or Steam, ~$35 — this course
  cannot be done with the free demo, and honesty obliges us to say that
  before you read three chapters). The course pins version **2.0.77**;
  any machine that runs the game comfortably is enough, no expansion
  required.
- **Python 3.11 or newer** and a terminal you're comfortable pasting
  commands into.
- About **30 minutes** for setup, once.

Nothing else from Factorio's world is required: no prior knowledge of
its technology tree, no combat (our worlds have no enemies), no rocket.
The course uses perhaps a dozen of the game's hundreds of mechanics, and
this chapter lists all of them.

## One-time setup

```sh
git clone git@github.com:MetaCoding-io/FactorioResearch.git
cd FactorioResearch
pip install -e '.[dev]'     # the quotes matter in zsh

# tell fisl where Factorio lives (add to your shell profile):
export FACTORIO_BIN=/path/to/factorio/bin/x64/factorio
```

The FISL measurement mods never need manual installation — every run
copies them into its own isolated workspace automatically.

## How a lab session works

Every lab follows the same operational rhythm:

1. In a terminal: `fisl run scenarios/factory-physics/<lab>`. This
   compiles the experiment, starts a private Factorio server from the
   lab's pristine baseline world, and prints a port number.
2. `fisl run` also prints a **ready-to-paste client command** (correct
   port and mod directory included) — copy it into a second terminal and
   the game opens straight into the lab.
3. In-game you'll spawn on the lab floor. The **FISL panel** (top left)
   shows READY. Walk around, look at everything, build if the lab calls
   for it — **the experiment clock does not start until you press Start
   Experiment.** The READY world is your practice range: nothing you do
   before Start is measured, and a fresh `fisl run` always begins from
   the same pristine world.
4. Press **Start Experiment** and operate. Two rules are enforced, not
   suggested: there is no pause (the clock is simulation ticks), and
   disconnecting mid-run aborts the run — data preserved, run marked
   aborted. Aborting is cheap; just run again.
5. When the final phase ends, the panel shows your results, and
   `fisl report runs/<run_id>` prints the full measurement record.

## The controls — all of them

Factorio has hundreds of keybindings. The course uses these (defaults
shown; Settings → Controls lists them all):

| You want to | Do |
|---|---|
| walk | **W A S D** |
| open / close your inventory | **E** (also closes most windows) |
| open a machine or chest | **left-click** it |
| take items from a chest | click items in its window (shift-click moves a stack) |
| place the item in your hand | **left-click** the ground |
| rotate the item in your hand (or a placed entity under the cursor) | **R** |
| empty your hand | **Q** (over an entity, **Q** instead copies it into your hand — handy) |
| remove an entity | **hold right-click** on it until it pops into your inventory |
| set a machine's recipe | open it, pick the recipe from its panel |
| see what everything is doing | **Alt** — toggles the info overlay; the course's figures assume it's on |
| drag a circuit wire | **Alt+R** (red) or **Alt+G** (green) puts the wire tool in your hand; click one entity, then the other |
| fullscreen | **Alt+Enter** |

Two mechanics deserve a sentence each, because labs from Lab 3 onward
lean on them:

- **Inserters have a direction.** An inserter grabs from the tile
  *behind* itself and drops *in front*; with the Alt overlay on, the
  arrow shows the drop direction. When a lab says "splice a chest into
  the belt," that means: remove one belt tile, place the chest there,
  and place one inserter feeding the chest and one taking from it —
  arrows pointing along the original flow.
- **Wires have a reach** (9 tiles). A wire that would stretch further
  simply doesn't connect — the game won't stop you from *trying*, and an
  unconnected control wire silently controls nothing. Check your
  connections visually. (This course's own reference solutions got
  burned by exactly this; you will read that story in Lab 3.)

## Reading the factory floor

The labs describe Factorio's objects in plant-floor language. The
dictionary, once:

| In the game | In the course | Role |
|---|---|---|
| transport belt | conveyor | moves material; **holds inventory in transit** |
| fast inserter | material handler | moves items between neighbors; has direction |
| assembling machine 1/2/3 | workstation (slow / medium / fast) | transforms material by a recipe, at a fixed rate |
| wooden / steel chest | buffer store | holds inventory in place |
| blue **source port** | receiving dock | where material enters the system — the declared boundary |
| orange **sink port** | shipping dock | where finished goods leave — the other boundary |
| toolbox chest (near spawn) | maintenance crib | the parts you're allowed to redesign with; never part of any measurement |
| constant / decider combinator | controller (PLC) | reads signals, applies a rule, drives equipment |
| substation, solar panel | power distribution | keep everything energized; in these labs you can ignore them |

The two ports are FISL bench equipment: indestructible, not openable,
not yours to move. They *are* the system boundary you'll read about in
every lab.

## Which labs need which hands

- **Labs 0–2**: walking and watching. Genuinely none of the building
  skills — your first three labs are safe territory to learn the
  controls in.
- **Labs 3–4**: placing and removing entities, the chest splice, a
  machine swap, and your first circuit wire.
- **Labs 5–6**: combinators and enable conditions — the deepest game
  skill the course uses, introduced by the lab chapters when needed.

If you're nervous about the hands: the next chapter, *The Practice
Range*, is a dedicated sandbox with six graded drills covering every
manipulation above — and any lab's READY floor also works as free
practice space that resets completely on the next run.
